prose_changes.old: In the middle of the eleventh century a circle of reformers around Pope Leo IX set out to free the church from the lay lords who appointed its bishops and sold its offices. And ended by claiming for the papacy an authority no bishop of Rome had exercised before. Gregory VII's Dictatus Papae of 1075 asserted, among much else, that the pope alone could depose an emperor. The resulting Investiture Contest ran for half a century and produced the extraordinary scene of Emperor Henry IV waiting in the snow outside Canossa. What followed was a working papal monarchy. Canon law codified, legates everywhere, a run of great councils at the Lateran, and under Innocent III, who reigned from 1198 to 1216, a papacy that arbitrated between kings, authorized the new friars, called crusades, and in 1215 legislated at the Fourth Lateran Council for the whole Latin church — from the definition of the eucharist to the requirement that every Christian confess once a year.
prose_changes.new: In the middle of the eleventh century, a circle of reformers around Pope Leo IX set out to free the church from lay lords. These lords chose its bishops and sold its offices. The reformers ended by claiming for the papacy a power no bishop of Rome had held before. Gregory VII's Dictatus Papae of 1075 declared, among much else, that the pope may depose emperors. The Investiture Contest that followed ran for half a century. Its most famous scene came in 1077. The German king Henry IV stood barefoot for three days at the gate of Canossa, begging the pope's pardon. What followed was a working papal monarchy. Canon law was gathered into codes, papal legates went everywhere, and great councils met at the Lateran. Innocent III, pope from 1198 to 1216, judged between kings, approved Francis of Assisi's first friars and called crusades. In 1215 his Fourth Lateran Council made law for the whole Latin church. Its rules ran from how the eucharist is defined to a rule that every Christian confess once a year.
prose_changes.reason: Three claims made more precise. 'The pope alone could depose an emperor': Dictatus Papae 12 (Mirbt no. 255, line 11202-11203) says only that he may depose emperors ('Quod illi liceat imperatores deponere'). 'Emperor Henry IV waiting in the snow': Gregory VII's own report (Mirbt no. 236, lines 10429-10431) has Henry, then king, barefoot and in wool for three days before the castle gate, begging mercy; no vendored text mentions snow. 'Authorized the new friars': Francis's Testament documents the pope's approval of the Franciscans (new link); no vendored or repo-cited source shows Innocent III approving the Dominicans, who were approved in 1216 (the Dominican entry's own date), so the sentence now names Francis's friars only. The whole paragraph was rewritten for reading level (it opened with a sentence fragment, 'And ended by claiming...'); every other fact is kept.

prose_changes.old: A circle of reformers around Pope Leo IX set out in the mid-eleventh century to free the church from lay lords who appointed its bishops and sold its offices, and ended by claiming for the papacy an authority no bishop of Rome had held before — Gregory VII's Dictatus Papae of 1075 asserted that the pope alone could depose an emperor, producing the Investiture Contest and the scene of Emperor Henry IV waiting in the snow at Canossa. What followed was a working papal monarchy, with canon law codified in Gratian's Decretum and legates and councils across Latin Christendom. Under Innocent III, the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 legislated for the whole Latin church, from the definition of the eucharist to a requirement that every Christian confess once a year.

The reformers ended by claiming for the papacy a power no bishop of Rome had held before. Gregory VII's Dictatus Papae of 1075 declared that the pope may depose emperors. The Investiture Contest followed. In 1077 the German king Henry IV stood barefoot for three days at the gate of Canossa. What came after was a working papal monarchy. Canon law was gathered in Gratian's Decretum, and legates and councils reached across the Latin West. Under Innocent III, the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 made law for the whole Latin church. Its rules ran from how the eucharist is defined to a rule that every Christian confess once a year.
prose_changes.reason: Same two corrections as in the description: Dictatus Papae 12 says the pope may depose emperors (not 'alone'), and Gregory VII's report has the king barefoot for three days at Canossa, with no snow. Rewritten whole for reading level; every other fact kept.

prose_changes.old: It never stopped: this is the Roman Catholic Church, and the institutional shape worked out here — a legally defined papal primacy, a professional canon law, a college of cardinals electing the pope, general councils legislating for the whole church — is substantially the shape it still has. Fourth Lateran's requirements of annual confession and Easter communion formed lay Catholic practice for the next seven centuries. So did darker parts of the same program: the same council imposed distinguishing dress on Jews and Muslims living in Christian territory, and the machinery of inquisition took its permanent form in these decades. The claims made here are also the ones the Reformation would eventually be a protest against. The same institution continued into the next era through Avignon and the Fifth Lateran Council.
prose_changes.new: It never stopped: this is the Roman Catholic Church. The shape the church took here is still, in large part, the shape it has. Its papal primacy is set in law. It has a trained body of canon law, cardinals who elect the pope, and general councils that make law for the whole church. Fourth Lateran's rules on yearly confession and Easter communion shaped lay Catholic life for the next seven centuries. So did darker parts of the same program. The same council made Jews and Muslims in Christian lands wear marked dress. The machinery of inquisition took its lasting form in these decades. The Reformation would later protest against these same claims. John Calvin named Gregory VII as the pope who first won the popes the rank of emperors. The same church carried on into the next era, through Avignon and the Fifth Lateran Council.
prose_changes.reason: The Reformation sentence now names the protest the vendored sources show: Calvin, Institutes IV.11.13, names Hildebrand (Gregory VII) as founder of the popes' imperial dignity (new link from the Reformed cities). The rest of the paragraph is rewritten for reading level with every fact kept. The canon on Jews' and Muslims' dress (Lateran IV c. 68) has no vendored source and is left standing; see escalations.

prose_changes.old: A transplanted Latin church with its own hierarchy: patriarchates of Jerusalem (1099, Greek patriarch expelled - the Schism lived on the ground) and Antioch; moves to Acre 1187, falls with it 1291
prose_changes.new: A transplanted Latin church with its own hierarchy. Latin patriarchs ruled at Jerusalem from 1099 and at Antioch, where the Greek patriarch withdrew about 1100 and a later one was thrown out in 1170. The Schism lived on the ground. The patriarchate moved to Acre in 1187 and fell with it in 1291.
prose_changes.reason: 'Greek patriarch expelled' at Jerusalem in 1099 is not supported by anything vendored: the 1869 editor's note (RHC Doc. arm. I, lines 15582-15584) says only that the patriarchate of Jerusalem was given to Daimbert. What the sources do show is at Antioch: the Greek patriarch John withdrew about two years after 1098 (the same note, lines 15575-15578), and Michael the Syrian records the Latins throwing out the Greek patriarch Athanasius after the 1170 earthquake (lines 46510-46511). The sentence now says that, and keeps 'the Schism lived on the ground', which those acts carry.

prose_changes.old: When the First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099 the conquerors did not simply add a diocese. They built a whole Latin church on top of an existing Christian landscape, erecting a Latin patriarchate of Jerusalem and expelling the Greek patriarch, and then another at Antioch. For nearly two centuries this transplanted hierarchy ran parishes, cathedrals and an enormous pilgrim traffic to the holy places, with the canons of the Holy Sepulchre at its center and a distinctive liturgy shaped by processions to the sites themselves. It governed a population that was mostly not Latin — Greek, Syriac, Armenian, Muslim — and its dealings with those communities ranged from workable accommodation to plain dispossession. When Jerusalem was lost in 1187 the patriarchate moved to Acre, and when Acre fell in 1291 the church of Outremer ended with it.
prose_changes.new: When the First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099, the conquerors did not simply add a diocese. They built a whole Latin church on top of an older Christian landscape. They set up a Latin patriarch in Jerusalem, and then another at Antioch. There the Greek patriarch soon left for Constantinople. For nearly two centuries this transplanted church ran parishes and cathedrals. It also served a huge flow of pilgrims to the holy places. The canons of the Holy Sepulchre stood at its center, with a liturgy shaped by processions to the sites themselves. Most of the people it ruled were not Latin. They were Greek, Syriac, Armenian and Muslim. Its dealings with them ran from workable peace to plain dispossession. When Jerusalem was lost in 1187 the patriarchate moved to Acre. When Acre fell in 1291, the church of Outremer ended with it.
prose_changes.reason: Same correction as the summary: 'expelling the Greek patriarch' of Jerusalem is replaced by what the vendored editor's note supports, the Greek patriarch of Antioch's withdrawal to Constantinople. Rewritten whole for reading level; every other fact kept ('workable accommodation' becomes 'workable peace').

It governed a population that was mostly not Latin — Greek, Syriac, Armenian, Muslim — with dealings that ranged from workable accommodation to outright dispossession. When Jerusalem was lost in 1187 the patriarchate moved to Acre, and when Acre fell in 1291 the church of Outremer ended with it.

The canons of the Holy Sepulchre stood at its center, with a liturgy shaped by processions to the holy places themselves. Most of the people it ruled were not Latin. prose_changes.old: It left no continuing institution in the East. When Acre fell, the Latin patriarchate of Jerusalem became a title without a diocese and stayed that way for more than five centuries, until it was restored as a working see in 1847. What survived instead is stone and story. The church of the Holy Sepulchre, largely rebuilt in this period, is substantially the building pilgrims enter today, and crusader castles and churches from Acre to Cyprus are among the best-preserved medieval buildings in the region. William of Tyre's history became the standard Western account of the crusades for centuries. The long memory of Outremer among Eastern Christians, who experienced it as occupation rather than liberation, is part of the legacy too.
prose_changes.new: It left no lasting church in the East. When Acre fell, the Latin patriarch of Jerusalem kept the title but lost the diocese. It stayed that way for more than five centuries, until the see came back to life in 1847. What survived instead is stone and story. The church of the Holy Sepulchre, largely rebuilt in this period, is mostly the building pilgrims enter today. Crusader castles and churches from Acre to Cyprus are among the best-kept medieval buildings in the region. William of Tyre's history became the standard Western account of the crusades for centuries. Eastern Christians remembered Outremer in different ways, and that memory is part of the legacy too. A Syriac chronicle tells how the Latins threw a Greek patriarch out of Antioch. An Armenian history recalls how the Franks of Jerusalem made their bond with the Armenians stronger than ever.
prose_changes.reason: 'Eastern Christians, who experienced it as occupation rather than liberation' spoke for all Eastern Christians with no source; the vendored witnesses disagree with each other. Michael the Syrian records the Latins throwing a Greek patriarch out of Antioch (RHC Doc. arm. I, lines 46510-46511); Kirakos of Gandzak records the Franks and their patriarch strengthening their friendship with the Armenians (lines 49737-49739). The sentence now reports both. Rewritten whole for reading level; every other fact kept. William of Tyre's reception sentence has no vendored source and is left standing; see escalations.

prose_changes.old: The Maronite Church is very much alive: one of the largest Eastern Catholic churches, the largest Christian community in Lebanon, and with a worldwide diaspora. The union begun here has held for eight centuries and made the Maronites the working model for later Eastern Catholic churches — communion with the papacy alongside a Syriac liturgy and a patriarch of their own. The Qadisha valley, where the monasteries and hermitages are carved into the cliff faces, remains a place of pilgrimage and is protected as world heritage.
prose_changes.new: The Maronite Church is very much alive. It is one of the largest Eastern Catholic churches and the largest Christian community in Lebanon. It also has a worldwide diaspora. The union begun here has held for eight centuries. It joined communion with the pope to a Syriac liturgy and a patriarch of the church's own. Later Eastern Catholic churches would share that pattern. The Qadisha valley, where monks carved their monasteries and hermit cells into the cliffs, is still a place of pilgrimage. It is protected as world heritage.
prose_changes.reason: 'Made the Maronites the working model for later Eastern Catholic churches' is an influence claim no vendored or repo-cited source supports. The sentence now says only that later Eastern Catholic churches shared the pattern, which is a likeness, not a line of descent. Rewritten whole for reading level; every other fact kept.

prose_changes.old: In the decades after the First Crusade, two kinds of institution fused into something the church had never authorized before. The Hospitallers began as a hospital in Jerusalem caring for pilgrims — they called the sick 'our lords the sick' — and only later took on a military role. The Templars began as a small band of knights guarding the pilgrim roads, took monastic vows, and were given a rule at the Council of Troyes in 1129. Bernard of Clairvaux wrote their defense, In Praise of the New Knighthood, arguing that a man who killed in this cause was not a homicide but, in his coinage, a malicide — a killer of evil. Both orders grew enormously rich, ran castles, estates and banking networks from the Latin East across Europe, and lost their reason for existing when Acre fell in 1291. The Templars were arrested in France in 1307, made to confess under torture, and suppressed in 1312.
prose_changes.new: In the decades after the First Crusade, two kinds of institution fused into something the church had never authorized before. The Hospitallers began as a hospital in Jerusalem caring for pilgrims. They called the sick 'our lords the sick', and only later took on a military role. The Templars began as a small band of knights guarding the pilgrim roads. They took monastic vows and were given a rule at the Council of Troyes in 1129. Bernard of Clairvaux wrote their defense, In Praise of the New Knighthood. He argued that a man who killed in this cause was not a homicide but, in his own coined word, a malicide: a killer of evil. Both orders grew enormously rich. They ran castles, estates and banking networks from the Latin East across Europe, and lost their reason for existing when Acre fell in 1291. The Templars were arrested in France in 1307 and made to confess under torture. In 1312 Pope Clement V abolished their order for ever.

escalations: For Mark (the open item 'Well-known facts with no vendored source', logged in Open-Gaps in the era-2 pass): five no-entry claims in this group are standard history but have no vendored or repo-cited source. The brief says to qualify such claims. I left them standing, because 'may have' on a council canon that is well known would mislead readers, and on the dress rule it would soften one of the darker facts the text rightly states.
